# Energy and Its Units — 1.1 What Is Energy?

<!-- ExamScribe draft. Chapter ch01, section part 1.1, pages 1–3. Source: chapters/ch01/source/1.1.md -->

::: concept T-energy
term: Energy
definition: [p.1: "Energy is the capacity to supply heat or do work."]
plain: Energy is what lets something heat another object or do work, and work means pushing matter over a distance. [p.1: "Work is done when a force moves matter through a distance."]
why: Nearly every chemical or physical change comes with a change in energy. [p.1: "Chemical changes and physical changes are almost always accompanied by changes in energy."]
misconception: Wrong: energy gets used up when it changes form. | Right: energy only changes form; it is never created or destroyed. [p.2: "Energy can be converted from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed."]
ai-mnemonic: Energy is "H or W": it can supply Heat or do Work.
:::

::: concept T-kinetic-energy
term: Kinetic energy
definition: [p.1: "Kinetic energy is the energy that an object possesses because of its motion."]
plain: Anything that moves has kinetic energy, and how much it has depends on both its mass and its speed. [p.1: "The kinetic energy of an object depends on both its mass and its speed"]
example: A rolling ball, a flowing river and a vibrating molecule all have kinetic energy. [p.1: "A rolling ball, a flowing river, and a vibrating molecule all have kinetic energy."]
misconception: Wrong: doubling the speed doubles the kinetic energy. | Right: doubling the speed multiplies the kinetic energy by four, because the speed is squared. [p.1: "Because the speed is squared, doubling the speed of an object multiplies its kinetic energy by four."]
:::

::: formula EQ-1.1
name: Kinetic energy of a moving object
latex: KE = \frac{1}{2} m v^2
where: KE = kinetic energy; m = mass of the object (kg); v = its speed (m/s). [p.1: "where m is the mass of the object in kilograms and v is its speed in meters per second"]
holds-when: UNSURE: the book gives no conditions for this formula
source: [p.1: "The kinetic energy of an object depends on both its mass and its speed:"]
check: KE = 1/2 * m * v^2
rearrange: v = sqrt(2 * KE / m)
rearrange: m = 2 * KE / v^2
:::

::: concept T-potential-energy
term: Potential energy
definition: [p.2: "Potential energy is the energy that an object possesses because of its position, composition, or condition."]
plain: Potential energy is energy an object has because of where it is, what it is made of, or its condition. [p.2: "because of its position, composition, or condition"]
example: A ball held above the ground has gravitational potential energy, and a battery stores chemical potential energy. [p.2: "A ball held above the ground has gravitational potential energy, and a battery stores chemical potential energy in the arrangement of its atoms."]
:::

::: concept T-law-of-conservation-of-energy
term: Law of conservation of energy
definition: [p.2: "Energy can be converted from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed. This principle is called the law of conservation of energy."]
plain: Energy can change form, for example from potential to kinetic energy, but it is never created or destroyed. [p.2: "Energy can be converted from one form to another, but it is never created or destroyed."] [p.2: "As it rolls down, potential energy is converted to kinetic energy."]
:::

::: concept T-thermal-energy
term: Thermal energy
definition: [p.2: "Thermal energy is the kinetic energy associated with the random motion of these particles."]
plain: Thermal energy is the motion energy of the atoms and molecules in matter, which are always moving randomly. [p.2: "The atoms and molecules in any sample of matter are in constant random motion."]
example: Hot tea has more thermal energy than the same tea after it cools, because its molecules move faster on average. [p.2: "A cup of hot tea has more thermal energy than the same cup of tea after it has cooled, because its molecules move faster on average."]
:::

::: figure FIG-1.1
what: A ball on a hill has the most potential energy at the top; as it rolls down, that potential energy turns into kinetic energy. [p.2: "A ball at the top of a hill has maximum potential energy. As it rolls down, potential energy is converted to kinetic energy."]
:::

::: worked-example WE-1.1
title: Calculating Kinetic Energy
source: Example 1.1 [p.3: "A 0.500-kg ball rolls at a speed of 4.00 m/s."]
problem: Find the kinetic energy of a 0.500 kg ball rolling at 4.00 m/s. [p.3: "A 0.500-kg ball rolls at a speed of 4.00 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?"]
step: Use the kinetic energy formula KE = ½mv² (Equation 1.1).
step: Substitute m = 0.500 kg and v = 4.00 m/s.
step: Square the speed first: (4.00 m/s)² = 16.0 m²/s².
step: Multiply: ½ × 0.500 kg × 16.0 m²/s² = 4.00 J.
calc: v2 = (4.00[m/s])^2 => 16.0[m^2/s^2]
calc: KE = 1/2 * 0.500[kg] * v2 => 4.00[J]
result: The ball's kinetic energy is 4.00 J. [p.3: "KE = ½ × 0.500 kg × (4.00 m/s)² = 4.00 J."]
:::

::: question Q-1.1-01
type: mcq
bloom: understand
ask: Which statement correctly tells kinetic energy apart from potential energy?
option A: Kinetic energy comes from motion; potential energy comes from position, composition, or condition.
option B: Kinetic energy is stored in batteries; potential energy belongs to moving objects.
option C: Both kinds of energy depend only on an object's speed.
option D: Potential energy can supply heat or do work, but kinetic energy cannot.
answer: A
why: The book defines kinetic energy by motion and potential energy by position, composition, or condition. [p.1: "Kinetic energy is the energy that an object possesses because of its motion."] [p.2: "Potential energy is the energy that an object possesses because of its position, composition, or condition."]
why-not B: It swaps the two: a battery stores chemical potential energy. [p.2: "a battery stores chemical potential energy in the arrangement of its atoms"]
why-not C: Only kinetic energy depends on speed; potential energy depends on position, composition, or condition.
why-not D: Every form of energy is a capacity to supply heat or do work. [p.1: "Energy is the capacity to supply heat or do work."]
covers: LO-1.1-1, T-kinetic-energy, T-potential-energy
:::

::: question Q-1.1-02
type: numeric
bloom: apply
ask: A 2.00 kg cart moves at 3.00 m/s. What is its kinetic energy in joules?
calc: KE = 1/2 * 2.00[kg] * (3.00[m/s])^2 => 9.00[J]
answer: 9.00[J]
why: Kinetic energy depends on the mass and on the speed squared. [p.1: "The kinetic energy of an object depends on both its mass and its speed"] [p.1: "Because the speed is squared, doubling the speed"]
covers: LO-1.1-2, EQ-1.1
:::

::: question Q-1.1-03
type: cloze
bloom: remember
ask: ____ is the kinetic energy associated with the random motion of atoms and molecules.
answer: Thermal energy
why: This is the book's definition of thermal energy. [p.2: "Thermal energy is the kinetic energy associated with the random motion of these particles."]
covers: LO-1.1-3, T-thermal-energy
:::

::: question Q-1.1-04
type: tf
bloom: understand
ask: Doubling an object's speed doubles its kinetic energy.
answer: false
why: The speed is squared, so doubling it multiplies the kinetic energy by four. [p.1: "Because the speed is squared, doubling the speed of an object multiplies its kinetic energy by four."]
covers: LO-1.1-2, EQ-1.1
:::
